nameStory: The daisy brittle star gets its charming name from its distinctive appearance — when viewed from above, its central disc and five radiating arms create a pattern that resembles a daisy flower. The 'brittle' part of its name comes from its fragile arms, which can easily break off when handled roughly or when the animal is trying to escape predators.
description: The daisy brittle star is a fascinating sea creature that looks like a cross between a starfish and a flower. It has a central disc (body) surrounded by five long, slender arms that can move independently like tiny snakes. These marine animals are typically small, with their central disc measuring about half an inch across and arms that can extend several inches. Unlike sea stars, brittle stars keep their arms distinctly separate from their body and use them primarily for movement rather than feeding.

idTips.label: Five flexible arms
idTips.description: Look for five long, snake-like arms that move independently and appear distinctly separate from the central body, unlike the broader arms of sea stars that blend into their body

idTips.label: Daisy-like pattern
idTips.description: The central disc often displays beautiful radiating patterns in various colors — browns, grays, reds, or oranges — that create a flower-like appearance when viewed from above

idTips.label: Small central disc
idTips.description: The round central body feels firm and is covered in small, bumpy scales that give it a slightly rough texture, typically about the size of a large pea

idTips.label: Fragile arms
idTips.description: The arms break off easily when touched — handle gently! They feel smooth and flexible, almost like tiny segmented worms

idTips.label: Active movement
idTips.description: Unlike sea stars that move slowly, brittle stars are surprisingly quick and will rapidly snake their arms to scurry under rocks or into crevices when disturbed

habitat: Look for daisy brittle stars in rocky intertidal zones and shallow subtidal waters along New England's coast, particularly in Maine and northern New Hampshire. They love to hide in crevices between rocks, under seaweed, or beneath overturned stones in tide pools. You'll often find them in areas with good water circulation, from the low tide zone down to deeper waters where the bottom is rocky or has plenty of hiding spots.

seasonality.spring: Brittle stars become more active as water temperatures rise, making them easier to spot during spring low tides when they venture out from winter hiding spots.
seasonality.summer: Peak observation time! They're most active and visible during summer low tides, often found moving across tide pool bottoms or hiding just under the edges of rocks.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek deeper shelter. Look for them in the deeper parts of tide pools and more protected rocky crevices.
seasonality.winter: Much less visible as they retreat to deeper waters or well-protected rocky hiding spots. Best found by carefully checking under larger rocks in the lowest tide zones.

funFact: Daisy brittle stars can regenerate their entire arm from just a tiny piece left attached to their body — and the broken-off arm can wiggle around for several minutes to distract predators while the brittle star escapes!
confusionNotes: Daisy brittle stars are most commonly confused with small sea stars, but remember: brittle star arms move like snakes and break off easily, while sea star arms move slowly and are firmly attached. Think 'brittle stars are wiggly, sea stars are sluggish.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name, brittle stars aren't actually stars at all — they're more closely related to sea urchins than to sea stars (starfish), and they belong to a completely different group of animals called ophiuroids, which means 'snake tails' in reference to their writhing arms.
compareHints: The daisy brittle star is the only Ophiopholis species in New England waters, making it unique in its genus here. Compared to other brittle stars in the region, it's distinguished by its particularly decorative, daisy-like disc patterns and its preference for rocky intertidal zones rather than sandy or muddy bottoms. Its arms are also relatively shorter and stouter compared to some of the more delicate brittle star species found in deeper New England waters.
